chunks: Rotary encoder and speed measurement. The question: What is a rotary encoder? How can it be used to measure motor speed?
A rotary encoder turns shaft rotation into electrical signals. The common type is an incremental quadrature encoder.
It outputs two on-off signals (square waves), A and B, that are a quarter of a cycle apart.
Counting the edges gives how far the shaft turned, and which wave comes first gives the direction. Dividing the count change by the elapsed time gives speed.
An absolute encoder outputs a unique code at each angle instead.
Picture a striped belt sliding past two eyes that are placed a quarter of a stripe apart. As the belt moves one way, the first eye sees each stripe edge first.
Move the belt the other way and the second eye sees it first. So the order tells you direction.
Every change at either eye is an edge you can count, so one stripe gives four counts.
Forward rotation: A rises first, then B rises a quarter cycle later. Each of the four edges per cycle is a count, so one line equals four counts.
If the shaft reverses, B leads A and the same state machine counts down.
Lines (PPR): how many cycles of channel A occur per revolution. Quadrature: two signals 90° apart. Their order gives the direction.
CPR: counts per revolution after decoding every edge, which is 4 times the lines. Index pulse (Z): one pulse per revolution, used for homing.
Hardware quadrature counter: a timer mode that counts up and down by itself, without the program handling each edge.
Take a 1024-line encoder decoded on all edges, so CPR is 4 times 1024 equals 4096 . At 3000 rpm, that is 50 rev/s, or 204,800 counts per second.
Read the counter every 1 milliseconds and you get about 205 counts. One count is 60 over (4096 times 0. 001) equals 14. 65 rpm, which is 0. 49% at this speed.
At 30 rpm the same window holds only about 2 counts, so the speed estimate hops in steps. That is the whole idea.
"A rotary encoder converts shaft rotation into electrical pulses.

An incremental quadrature encoder gives two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees apart, so the phase order gives direction and counting every edge gives four times the line count, plus an index pulse once per rev.
For speed I count edges over a fixed window, rpm equals 60 times counts over CPR times window, or time between edges at low speed.
Absolute encoders give a unique code for each angle."
